newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW-Dutch telecom Big Bang offers big prizes.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Dutch telecom Big Bang offers big prizes.

text.p: Dutch telephone users face a dizzying array of offers and deals over the coming months as the Netherlands liberalises voice telephony from Tuesday, and every one can win, said a phone company president.
Consumers will clearly benefit from lower prices and new services as competition heats up, said Esprit Telecom president Michael Potter in an interview.
But the new efficiencies which could be forced on erstwhile fixed-line voice monopoly player Koninklijke PTT Nederland NV could also bring industry-wide benefits, said Potter.

"As prices come down the overall market will be stimulated. Because the overall market is going to be stimulated and you'll get a tremendous increase in traffic, the Big Bang in Holland allows for a win-win situation for all competitors," he said.
"The consumer should be very happy. It's only taken about 100 years to get choices... in the Netherlands," said Potter.

From Tuesday the Netherlands is liberalising fixed line voice telephony, allowing a range of competitors the chance to tackle KPN head-on before the January 1998 liberalisation of European voice telephony.

Ranging against KPN is Enertel, a grouping of energy companies and cable television ventures with 5,000 kilometres (3,100 miles) of optical fibre and potential access to 3.7 million Dutch cable TV households.

Enertel entered the arena on Monday with details of international services to individual and small-to-medium sized business operators, offering savings of up to 25 percent to heavy users on existing international KPN services.
National offers are likely to be available some time in 1998, an Enertel spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

Telfort, the partnership of British Telecom Plc and the Dutch national railway firm, Nederlandse Spoorwegen, plans initially to offer data, corporate voice and virtual private networks as well as international voice and data services.
It sees revenues of 200 million guilders in 1997 and hopes to increase that tenfold in five to seven years, gaining Dutch market share of 10-15 percent over the next five years.

Esprit, one of the pioneers of telecoms competition in the Netherlands, has been active in the country since 1993 offering specialised services to businesses. It now plans to offer wider access to its system via a short-code dial-in process.
Esprit's Potter said the use of short-code systems was a step forward but not full and open access to the nation's telecoms infrastructure.

"Customers are being asked to dial special digits, one of the numbers we have is 1680. If it was the other way around, if you wanted to use PTT and you had to dial 1680 all of a sudden PTT's revenue would drop, just because people get lazy and people forget to use the numbers," Potter said.
"Why should new entrants be discriminated against? it isn't a level playing field and that's a significant issue," he added.

Potter said KPN faced big challenges as new competitors streamed into the market, forcing it to find new efficiencies and exploit its national network aggresssively as telecom prices to consumers reflected underlying costs ever more closely.

"PTT has a lot of strengths, they have very good technical people and they have a very good network throughout the Netherlands, the question is are they as efficient as they should be?" asked Potter, drawing parallels with BT which has become a world telecoms player since privatisation in the 1980s.

"Has PTT Netherlands been as aggressive in trying to get to the same levels of efficiency as BT? If not then they may feel some pain in the market as they go forward. Also the new entrants who don't really have the full economies of scale might have a more difficult time," Potter said.

"I think that if PTT can adapt to the new changes there's no reason it can't be a win-win situation for most of the players in the marketplace. If players are focused and commercial they should be able to prosper," he said.
